title: Artemis I moon rocket at Launch Complex 39B, Kennedy Space Center, Florida, United States
caption: The universe is calling
subtitle: World Space Week begins
description:
First, you build a rocket. Then you ask it to leave Earth, fly to the moon, survive the trip and bring its spacecraft home. Simple, right? Well, not quite. World Space Week, observed every 4-10 October, celebrates the science that makes missions like this possible. The United Nations established the observance in 1999 to commemorate Sputnik 1's launch on 4 October 1957, and the entry into force of the Outer Space Treaty on 10 October 1967. This year's theme, 'Rocket Revolution,' focuses on the evolving technology driving space exploration.
Seen in today's image, Artemis I put plenty of that technology to work. On 16 November 2022, NASA launched an uncrewed Orion spacecraft aboard the Space Launch System from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, United States. Orion flew around the moon, covering about 2.3 million kilometres over 25.5 days. No astronauts climbed aboard this time. That was the point. Artemis I had one job: prove the system could make the journey before people took the next one.

title: Adélie penguins, Antarctica
caption: Slide into adventure
subtitle: Adélie penguins, Antarctica
description:
What can a 70-centimetre-tall bird teach us about life? Quite a lot. The Adélie penguin offers a lesson plan packed with resourcefulness, resilience and a little mischief. Found along the Antarctic coast, the species was named after Adèle, the wife of French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville, during the expedition that encountered the penguins in 1840.
Adélie penguins are famous for building nests from pebbles. Males collect stones to attract mates, but some also help themselves to pebbles from neighbouring nests. Small but surprisingly feisty, they defend their territory with their flippers when challenged. When crossing snowy terrain, they have another clever trick: they lie on their bellies and slide across the ice, a move known as tobogganing.
In the water, Adélies are agile swimmers, reaching speeds of several kilometres per hour as they hunt for food or evade predators such as leopard seals. So, today's lesson? Adapt, stay determined and, when necessary, go with the slide.

title: Danxia landform, Zhangye National Geopark, Gansu, China
caption: Earth's story in stripes
subtitle: International Geodiversity Day
description:
What if a mountain range could show you its geological history in stripes? At Zhangye National Geopark in China, the rocks do exactly that. Ridges roll across the landscape in bands of red, orange, yellow, brown and other earthy tones. Known as the Danxia landform, this striking landscape was shaped by layers of sedimentary rock deposited over geological time. Tectonic forces later lifted and folded the rocks, while weathering and erosion carved them into ridges, cliffs, gullies and peaks.
The name Danxia literally translates to rosy clouds. The colours come from the rocks themselves, with minerals and chemical processes contributing to the different shades. Iron oxides, for instance, are responsible for much of its characteristic red colouring, while variations in minerals and sediment create its broader palette.
Designated as a UNESCO Global Geopark in 2020, Zhangye is located in Gansu, a region linked to the ancient Silk Road. For International Geodiversity Day, it is a colourful reminder that Earth's best artwork is rock-solid.

title: Moss-covered rocks in Puzzlewood, Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire, England
caption: Puzzled? Follow the trail
subtitle: Puzzlewood, Forest of Dean, Gloucestershire, England
description:
What if a forest could keep you guessing at every turn? At Puzzlewood, near Coleford in the Forest of Dean, England, winding paths lead through twisted trees, moss-covered rocks and deep stone ravines. Its unusual rock formations, known as scowles, are natural geological features that were exposed and modified over time and later exploited for iron ore mining during the Roman period and possibly earlier. In 1848, a worker discovered more than 3,000 Roman-era coins hidden in earthenware jars inside a rock cavity, turning the woodland into a real-life treasure hunt.
Around 2.4 kilometres of paths, wooden bridges and stone walkways guide visitors through the rugged landscape. Puzzlewood has also starred on screen, appearing in 'Star Wars: The Force Awakens,' 'Doctor Who,' 'Merlin' and 'Cursed.' Local lore links its gnarled trees and mysterious atmosphere to JRR Tolkien's Middle-earth forests, although there is no definitive proof.

title: Octopus in defensive posture, Mayotte, Indian Ocean
caption: Now you 'sea' me...
subtitle: World Octopus Day
description:
Something has clearly crossed a line. Off the coast of Mayotte in the Indian Ocean, this octopus has adopted a defensive posture that says: whatever is approaching should reconsider its life choices.
It's a warning octopuses can deliver with style. Instead of armour, they rely on transformation. Together, tiny muscular structures called papillae and pigment-filled chromatophore cells let them change colour, pattern and even skin texture within seconds. The result is an animal that can resemble rocks, coral, algae or shadows. It doesn't simply blend into its surroundings. It becomes them.
And camouflage is only the opening act. Octopuses can vanish in a cloud of ink, squeeze through openings barely larger than their beak, solve puzzles and explore with arms that contain most of their neurons. In a sense, each arm has a mind of its own. World Octopus Day celebrates one of the ocean's great evolutionary oddities: three hearts, eight arms, blue blood. Nature really went off script with this one.

title: View of the Sanguinaires Islands from Corsica, France
caption: Corsica's rocky outposts
subtitle: View of the Sanguinaires Islands from Corsica, France
description:
Just off the coast of Corsica, France, the Sanguinaires Islands rise from the Mediterranean as a small archipelago of four rugged, rocky islands. Viewed from a historic watchtower, they sit at the entrance to the Gulf of Ajaccio. Steep cliffs, centuries-old landmarks and sweeping sea views have drawn visitors to the area for generations. Though the farthest island lies only about 2 kilometres from shore, the archipelago feels surprisingly remote, surrounded by open water and shaped by wind, waves and salt spray.
Visitors can reach Mezu Mare, the largest island, via authorised boat services and explore its designated footpaths. Elsewhere, protected habitats provide refuge for nesting seabirds and hardy Mediterranean plants adapted to dry, windswept conditions. A lighthouse on Mezu Mare stands as a reminder of the archipelago's long maritime history and strategic position at the entrance to the gulf. Today, the Sanguinaires Islands offer dramatic scenery, wildlife and traces of a rich seafaring heritage, creating one of Corsica's most memorable natural landscapes.

title: Double-crested cormorants over Monterey Bay, California, United States
caption: Life along the flyway
subtitle: World Migratory Bird Day
description:
World Migratory Bird Day celebrates one of nature's greatest journeys. Observed each year in May and October, the global campaign reflects migration patterns around the world and highlights the importance of protecting the habitats and flyways that birds depend on. 'Every Bird Counts—Your Observations Matter!' is the 2026 theme, emphasising how observations by individuals and communities can contribute to bird research, monitoring and conservation, helping scientists better understand migration.
Today's image captures double-crested cormorants flying above the waves of Monterey Bay, California, United States. Widespread across North America, these adaptable seabirds may migrate or remain year-round, depending on the population. Along California's coast, bays, wetlands and estuaries provide important habitat for birds travelling the Pacific Flyway. For many species, these ecosystems support journeys spanning vast distances. Each sighting helps reveal these migrations and reminds us that even a single bird can be part of a much larger story.

title: Glade Creek Grist Mill, Babcock State Park, West Virginia, United States
caption: Where autumn turns the wheel
description: Surrounded by a patchwork of red, orange and gold, Glade Creek Grist Mill stands above the rocky waters of Glade Creek in West Virginia's Babcock State Park, United States. Although it looks like a relic from the pioneer era, the mill is actually a carefully crafted tribute to Appalachia's milling heritage.
